utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Margetts, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're ready to call Witness Number 76. Mr. President, there is one matter that arises with this witness and that is that we are not certain as to whether this witness has any concerns as to his security because we haven't had the opportunity to speak with him. Our recommendation may be or our suggestion may be that he be called into the court and we possibly start in private session. And we inquire with him as to whether there are any objective bases for any security concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that there is no objection from the Defence teams to such an approach? Then we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Buhin, may I invite you to stand. Mr. Buhin, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. Please be seated. Mr. Buhin, you will be first examined by Mr. Margetts. Mr. Margetts is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin. Mr. Buhin, do you recall that on the 15th and 16th of September in 2001, and again on the 9th of March, 2002, you met with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And do you recall that at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, it is a good tradition that we first have the name and date of birth on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, apologies, I neglected just one matter and that is you could you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: My name is Stjepan Buhin. I was born on July 1st, 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Buhin, I referred to meetings that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you recall that at the conclusion of those meetings that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could please have 65 ter 5491 brought up on the screen. That is a statement of Mr. Buhin. Mr. Buhin has not had the advantage of seeing this statement in recent days. So if I could, if the court usher could please provide Mr. Buhin with a copy of the statement in Croatian. And, Mr. President, you will note that the original statement is in Croatian, and we have a translation of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, if you could look at the document before you. And are you able to confirm, looking at that document there, that that is the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. My signature is on each page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, it's a statement of approximately 6 pages and, Mr. President, it may be a convenient time for Mr. Buhin to review that statement, since he has not had the opportunity to do so prior to this time. So Mr. Buhin, would you be able to read through that statement, please, and just read it carefully and then indicated to us whether it accurately reflects the statement that you made in March 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, that might take some time, isn't it, to read a six-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first inquire into the -- the signatures and what was -- whether he read it at that time or whether it was read to him. Mr. Buhin, when you gave this statement, have you read the -- the version which is in front of you, the Croatian version of this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a minor problem with this. My first interview, which was in September 2001, was conducted via an interpreter, and it was written down in English. Once the interview was over, I did not want to sign this because I didn't know what was written down and I can't speak any English. The second interview followed in 2002, in March, a similar procedure occurred. The interview was conducted through an interpreter and the statement was written down in English, and the room we had the interview in was really, really cold, so the interpreter, the woman who wrote down the statement, it was -- for her it was the first time to use this type of computer, so she made a lot of mistakes and this interview took quite a while. Once the statement was drafted, the investigators left us -- the two of us, there so that she could translate this back into Croatian and this took a while, and we were both freezing. Her fingers were totally stiff it was so cold. Once she finished the statement she read it back to me, and I signed this version, because I really was out of patience. I was also sorry for her, because it was so cold, so that once she read this back to me, I just signed it, and I believed it was all right, although I did not read it myself. And now I can see that there is only one statement, which would mean that this is one single statement from those two interviews, because I don't see two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that appears to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I suggest that we give the witness time to read the statement, not necessarily all of us here waiting for him. He might feel under pressure. Mr. Buhin, could you tell us, how much time would you approximately need to read the six pages? Would 20 minutes do or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then upon your return, upon our return, we would ask you whether this statement accurately reflects what you said at the time, whether that was in September or March is not of vital importance, I would say, so we'd like to know whether this reflects what you said at that time, and also whether it is accurate and in accordance with the truth, and we'll then also ask you whether you would give the same answers if the same questions were to be put to you today. I think this is not a good environment to quietly read the statement. We'll adjourn -- we'll have a pause until 3.00, so that you have a little bit over 25 minutes to read it, and afterwards please inform me, inform us whether -- what your answer is to the question is I just told you will be put to you. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 3.00. --- Break taken at 2.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, did you manage to review the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there -- first question, as I said before, does the statement accurately reflect what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. It has been quite a while. There are some minor things that I noticed. I'm not sure if I actually said these things at the time, but maybe I would phrase them a little differently now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest, there are a few - do I understand you well - a few matters which you'd like to raise. Then I will leave it to Mr. Margetts, if you tell Mr. Margetts where they can be found, then Mr. Margetts will further guide you through the document. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, if you could take us to the first paragraph where you indicated something may be phrased in a slightly different manner, indicate to the Court the correction that you'd like to make. Which page does that arise on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Buhin, if you could please give us the first few words of that paragraph so that we can locate it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: When I spoke with Josko Moric and Djurica Franjo they told me that my position would be above the police chief, in terms of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, will you see, and Mr. Registrar that is on page 3 of the English. And it's about the middle paragraph on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Buhin, if you could continue. And how would you rephrase any of the sentences in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: At the time I talked to the investigators, we probably didn't pay that much attention to these details. Therefore, this is -- a very simple explanation of what it means to be above the police chiefs in terms of rank. The role of the coordinators, and that's what we were, was advisory. We were high-ranking in the sense of providing advice, providing assistance as to how they would set up their administration and how they would organise their work. But the final executive decision was in the hands of those newly appointed chiefs, if there were differences of opinions in certain matters that always had to be dealt with at the level of the ministry. We didn't have the authority to take the final decision. That's one thing. And then three paragraphs down, Knin was a police administration in charge of the liberated territory in its entirety. And then it goes on to say both Baric and I were positioned higher up than Romanic, but this is not explained and that's the problem, and that's what I said. A higher position, yes, because we were from the ministry. But this was only in terms of instructions, in terms of coordination. The newly appointed chiefs were the ones who had final say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Buhin. I think that matter is clear. Are there any other paragraphs that would like to take us to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the bottom of page 3. When a case was reported that involved persons in army uniforms, we would report that to the criminal police and General Cermak would also find about that at daily meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Buhin -- Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 4 the second paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Buhin. And the further matters you'd like to address in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: This is something that will then be taken up by the military police, but as it continues, you can see that the military police would be informed so -- I apologise, actually, this is fine. Page 5, paragraph 2 up towards the top of the page. The civilian police were not allowed to check military vehicles or anyone in military uniform. These were instructions from the MUP or an order from the MUP. They were killings and looting committed by people in military uniforms, but our hands were tied. I don't know how this was interpreted at the time. This bit about our hands being tied. The uniformed police, we provided instructions for their work and guidance but they did their work, and that was that. Therefore, I don't know how this wording came about, in terms of the hands of the police being tied. The police did their work and did it just fine. Maybe not exactly in the way we would have liked to, but that is what the circumstances were. We were certainly trying to do our best to the extent it was possible at the time and be as professional as we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, this is not perfectly clear to me. The first line, the first sentence you say you were not allowed to check military vehicles or people in military uniform. That was an instruction or an order from the MUP and this line you were referring to says: "There were killings and looting committed by people in military uniforms but our hands were tied." Now, could you check or proceed against persons in military uniform that were suspected of killing and looting, or could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your hands were tied to the extent that you could not proceed against anyone in military uniform, even if you suspected that person of being involved in killing and looting. Is that how we have to understand this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not quite. If we had found or if we had been certain in a given situation that a certain person had committed a serious crime such as murder or robbery, the uniformed police would then have arrested this person and handed this person over to the military police. However, there were simply no situations like that. This is simply what the investigator asked me at that time. What if, what if you had found this, what if you had found that, what would you as police have done? If there had been any reliable or unambiguous information about that, we would have arrested the person and then handed the person over to the military police and other appropriate services, but there was nothing like that that actually happened. The civilian police were marked out. You could tell them from an afar. There weren't that many of us to begin with. And there was nothing like this that actually happened anywhere in the presence of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in the theoretical situation, that's what you described, you could have arrested someone suspected of having looted or having killed, but if that was a military person, you would have to hand them over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a small error. It's probably a copying error, third paragraph from the bottom up. Sacic would have known where the military police were doing their mopping-up operations. This should read: Special police and not military police. The military police, as far as I know, was not involved in any mopping-up operations. Rather, this was the job of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Any other paragraph which needs further attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not really noticed anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So apart from those corrections, that further information that have you provided to us, does this document set out that the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same statement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Probably not. My views are slightly different now as opposed to what they were back then. It has been quite some time, and the reasoning is now different. My interpretation of certain matters would now probably be different as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In terms of this statement, insofar as it refers to factual matters and events, is it an accurate depiction of those factual matters and events?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. So I just wanted to be clear in respect of those facts and events, if you were asked the same questions about those matters, would you give the same statement today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm -- not sure now to proceed here because I don't know that at the end of the day the Prosecution and the Defence at this point are going to agree as to what is fact in the statement and what is a conclusion, what's an opinion, so I -- I -- at this point would lodge an objection unless the Prosecution is going to take him through the statement and say, This specific fact you agree, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is not a very practical way of proceeding. Mr. Buhin, could you explain to us on what matters you have, as you said, your interpretation would now be different? Could you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult to say it like that. As far as any details are concerned that I might want to change. But I'm certain that there are quite many generalisations here. What if this had been the case, what if that would have been the case, then what should have followed as a result but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example -- could you give us an example on where you feel apparently uncomfortable with your statement, in respect of what you just told us? Could you take to us any ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to speak about specific examples in a hurry. I can't do this in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then suggest that we proceed and that in the next break, you will -- that you'll read it again and that you, after that break, point to us matters where you say -- or give an example of the kind of matters on which you say you may have changed your opinion. And then perhaps, for the time being, we proceed and a final decision on admission would then be delayed, but we proceed on the basis as if the statement was admitted. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And then of course we'll -- if necessary, read the summary at the time that we seek admission of the statement. Mr. President, I have one matter and it is to do to the first exhibit that I'd like to refer to. And if we could just go into private session for a short moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could please have 65 ter number 5266 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, on the right-hand side of the screen, you will see an organigram -- it is appearing rather small on my screen, Mr. Registrar. Possibly if we could enlarge the top of the organigram. Yes, Mr. Buhin, this is an organigram which was put together by the Office of the Prosecutor. And it shows the organisation of the Ministry of Interior in the Knin region for the period August to September 1995. And if you look down to the bottom right-hand corner, you'll see that your name appears there as a coordinator, and there's a broken line that -- that links your office, that of the police coordinators of Kotar-Knin, to the Zagreb authorities, in particular, Djurica Franjo and then subsequently Marijan Tomurad. Could you look at that organigram, and could you indicate to the Court whether or not you consider that that accurately sets out the organisation of the authorities in the Kotar-Knin region and their superiors during the period August to September 1995?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President. If this organigram, 65 ter 5266, could be given an exhibit number and entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please assign an exhibit number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P962 is admitted into evidence. Can we go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buhin, in the course of reviewing your statement, you indicated the nature of the role of the coordinators and the relationship that you had with the other police chiefs in the area. I'd like to deal with that matter a little further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I please have 65 ter 2786 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buhin, you'll see on the left-hand side of the screen there an Official Note, and I'd just like to ask you some preliminary questions in relation to that Official Note. And that is this. This note purports to be an Official Note that was prepared following an interview that was conducted with you on the 9th of October, 2001, by Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please move to page two of the B/C/S and similarly to page -- to the final page of the English which is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you'll see there there's a sign-off, or not a sign-off but at least the name of the gentleman Ivica Vesel. So my first question to you is this: Do you recall being interviewed by Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior officials, in particular, Mr. Vesel, on the 9th of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could move back, Mr. Registrar, to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Buhin, that in the -- there's a sentence that refers to the fact that this records information that you gave to the officials, and then there is a paragraph of approximately four lines, a further line, and then a second substantial paragraph which appears about in the middle of the page. Now, at the end of that paragraph there, there's a reference to the role of the coordinators and it says that the coordinators were appointed to coordinate, supervise and direct the work of police employees at the Knin police station. So that sentence there, is that correct, is that a correct characterization of the role of the coordinators?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. This document is not such a lengthy document and it -- at this time it is probably convenient if I give you an opportunity to read through it in its entirety and then just indicate to me whether it accurately records matters that it refers to.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: We can turn the page. I've read the Official Note. I just skimmed it, actually, and I'm surprised that my colleague, the police officer, wrote this lengthy document before -- because before I was invited to give an interview to the investigators of this court, I requested that a member of the civilian authorities of the Republic of Croatia also attend this interview, because I was afraid there may be some abuse of that interview. I asked, through my colleagues who worked at the ministry, for assistance but no one would assist me and then I was invited for this interview. The interview lasted about three to five minutes, with a colleague. He never took any notes. And I just thought this conversation was a mere formality, just to meet the formal aspects. Now that I see that this note was prepared, I suppose that he did it because somebody asked that of him, and some of the facts that were set forth here are incorrect. For instance, the incident in the village of Grubori, I don't recall -- I don't think that I would have said anything to this effect, as stated here. I wouldn't have said that it took two days before it was reported, nor did I say that there was rainfall on that day, so some of the things that he put in there must have been from some other forces and not based on what I said. When I returned to the MUP seat, to the headquarters of the MUP, and -- so this reference to my return to the MUP and that the relations cooled, I don't know what that would mean because there was no need for me to go back to Knin because another inspector had come there in the meantime. He was a traffic expert. And my colleague Baric remained there. He was also from the regular police, so that now there were more involved in regulating traffic. Now, the reference to my retirement also in this Official Note is not well explained. I retired because I wanted to and not because I had to and not because it would have been somebody else's wish. The conditions at the year when I decided to retire were favourable for me, and I took advantage of this, so I decided to retire and I did this of my own free will. Therefore, I think that this note was just drafted based on the recollections of what was said, and if you asked me, I would just discard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Buhin, for that lengthy answer. There's one matter I would like to refer to. We referred to the reference to the coordinators, and you indicated in your answer that there were certain aspects of the information relating to the incident in Grubori that you don't recall communicating to the official. What I would like to ask you is whether or not you recall indicating to the official the matters that appear from the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could refer to the first page of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see that five lines from the bottom, Mr. Buhin, there's a reference to 25 August 1995, and that says it is possible that the date was 25 August 1995. And then there's a reference to various events that occurred. And I'd just like you to read on that part of the statement or that part of that paragraph to the end of that paragraph and just tell me whether those events that are recorded there are matters that -- that you're aware of and that you communicated to Mr. Vesel. Looking at the part that says: "Namely, he remembers an incident that was indeed reported by UN members and continuing on until an investigation would be conducted the following day."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: This conversation was rather casual, the conversation that I had with this colleague. We just mentioned the event in Grubori. I don't think more than a few words were said about it. And I believe that he wrote this as he felt he should, because I couldn't have said any of these things to him nor do I recall these events. As far as I can remember, the complaint came in the morning hours. There was no need to wait for nightfall. There were no impediments of any sort. I can't tell you exactly at what time we received the complaint or the report. It was in the morning, sometime in the morning. When I learned of this, I ordered that two teams of civilian police patrols be sent to the site to determine what it was about. About midday I learned that the patrols had returned and that they were unable to find this village, the village of Grubori, or any bodies for that matter. I have to stress that this police came -- had come from different -- from other parts of the country. They did not know the area very well, nor could they rely on the local population and ask people for their way. They just had to rely on their own resources. The colleague Baric and I went to the UN headquarters, the UN police headquarters, discussed this or had a conversation with the police officers who had been on site and asked them to take us to the site and show us the bodies so that we could take the steps that were necessary. We agreed to do this in the afternoon hours, around 3.00 p.m., to allow us time to inform the police administration in Zadar, the crime police, and in order to make sure that an investigating judge would also attend. This is how these events unfolded. In the meantime, Zeljko Sacic, the deputy chief of the special police, also came to our headquarters. He was rather angry because he hadn't been informed of this, and he said that the mop-up operation had been conducted in that area. In other words, there was fighting going on. I tried to explain to him what information I had and what we had done up till then, but he claimed that even if there were any bodies, they would have been bodies of men who died in combat and that this would be handled by the civilian protection. In the meantime, I received a phone call from the ministry, from Josko Moric. I cannot tell you how he learned about this event. He was rather angry, and he said to me that I should not get involved in assignments that were not within my purview. I reiterate, I was responsible for the -- the regular police work and traffic regulation, whereas this work was really something that the crime police should handle. When the crime police -- since the crime police had been informed, I decided not to follow up on this, and I left this to the crime police to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. We will deal with some other documents later on relating to this matter and I will give you an opportunity to explain a little bit further in relation to some of those matters. Just following up now on that last issue, you said that you informed the crime police and earlier up in the answer, you said that the police administration in Zadar was informed. Who was informed in the police administration in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you for certain, but I believe it was the chief of the police administration, Ivo Cetina. A lot of time has passed since, and I don't have any notes here, but all -- all bits of information of this nature would go to him. We would send it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And you indicated that Mr. Moric suggested that this was a matter for the criminal police and not for you. When you received the information, did you immediately inform the Zadar criminal police. Or -- sorry. Did you immediately inform the Zadar police administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And when you heard about the matter, I think you indicated in your answer there it was in the morning. Did you hear about it on the same day that it occurred, or did you hear about it at any later time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: It was in the morning hours. I cannot be more precise. I was informed then by the police station chief, I think it was Mr. Mihic. He told me that he had been informed by the UN police of bodies that were found in Grubori village. How old these bodies were or how long they had been there, I didn't have any information as to the -- to that, and I just wanted to check the complaint that we received, or, rather the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you, Mr. Buhin. As I say we'll return to that topic a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in regard to this Official Note, I think the witness has indicated he has some reservations in relation to it. I just want to be sure that we have on record his confirmation of the specific sentence that we referred to, relating to the role of coordination. So I just would like to read that out to him again and that would avert the need to introduce this Official Note into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would object to that, Your Honour, because the witness didn't confirm that those statements in the Official Note are exactly the testimony or the conversation that he with the police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that is exactly the reason why Mr. Margetts does not want to tender the whole of the document into evidence. Is that -- Mr. Margetts, is that what was on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, my intention is to isolate the part relating to the role of the coordinators and then not to seek admission of the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. We'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, do we really need that -- sort a sentence out of the document? I'm not creating problems, but it seems a bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we see is that the document in some respects confirms what the witness tells us today. To that extent, the document has some corroborating value. Therefore, I'm -- it's not yet clear on my mind whether this is a document -- apart from whether we would accept everything that is said in this document, whether not tendering would not give us some thought on whether we might call this as Bench evidence but of course I have to discuss this first with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I just raise it in terms of practicalities because we have to deal with the information and know what we're precisely dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I do not know exactly what portion Mr. Margetts intends to read to the witness, and we'll see what remains from the document and whatnot. Little bit in the -- still in the dark. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, from our position I think our position is that we don't have an objection to the document coming in. It's not -- as long as we all understand that it is it not a witness statement per se it's an Official Note, and I think there have been other documents that have come in with other witnesses, with similar police accounts. The second point I wanted to make is while I agree with Your Honour's observation about the corroborative value of what he had said earlier, I'm not sure, and I sincerely say I'm not sure, what the OTP's position is on whether this is corroborative of he said or contradicts, and to that extent, then I just ask that it be put to the witness whatever the sentence is being used for in order to -- that we are clear in the future as to what the witness's position is with regard to that sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, a lot of words in relation to a matter you tried to resolve in a simple way, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As it turns out I have had the opportunity in -- while the submissions being made to check the transcript. In fact, the sentence found its way on to the transcript, in any event, at page 19, lines 10 to 16. So that averts the need for me to proceed, and I don't intend to seek admission of this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That accords with my idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed on this basis for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I'd like to ask you some questions about the military police, in particular, the role of the civilian police and the role of the military police. You will have seen in your statement that you've reviewed earlier today that you make reference to the role of the military police and the role of the civilian police. I'd like to refer you back to your statement and it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 5491. If we could refer to page 5 of the B/C/S, and it's also page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Buhin, that's from the top of page 5. If you could just read down to effectively the middle of the page. In the English, it starts at the third paragraph on the fifth page. And it's the sentence that starts: "When check-points were set up ..." Now, this is just a passage I'd like you to read, Mr. Buhin, and indicate whether you fully adopt that particular passage or whether any of those issues that you raised earlier in relation to interpretation arise in regard to -- to this first half of page 5.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Could you please just help me with how this paragraph begins. What are the words? What paragraph exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the paragraph at the top of the page that starts: "When check-points were set up ..."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So that paragraph. And the next two -- or the next three paragraphs. And you'll note that one of these paragraphs is one of the paragraphs you developed and you provided some extra information in relation to, earlier today.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Our wish was to be efficient and for -- for better work, we wanted the check-points of the military police and the civilian police to be at the same spot. However, in the early days, when we arrived there, this was impossible, and the military police check-points were always some 10 to 20 metres behind the civilian police check-points so that the civilian police stopped, intercepted, and searched the civilians whereas the military police stopped and searched military or people in uniforms. Why this was so, I wouldn't know. The military police probably had their own reasons for this. But when I subsequently thought about it a bit, it was probably more efficient or easier to do it this way so that everyone would do their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, if I could refer you past the second paragraph, which we already dealt with today and then past the third paragraph on page 5 of the version in front of you, and you could read from the paragraph that starts: "While I was working in the liberated area ..." and you could read down to the section that says: "But they refused ..." which is the next two paragraphs, although there is no line-break between them.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I think I've already explained this today. In the event that a vehicle with civilian plates had uniformed men in them, and in the event that they were stopped by the civilian police, they would always show their cards, military cards, to show that they were members of a certain unit of the HV. They also had documents to show about the goods that they were transporting, and of course such vehicles we would let through. There were questions by the investigator about this particular paragraph. The questions were very hypothetical. What would have happened if this was the case? I would like to reiterate, if the civilian police were to find a perpetrator in the course of committing a crime, we would detain such a person and hand them over to the military police. These events here, described here, only concern transport and crossing of check-points, and we would always let the military police handle that because it was not within our competence and we did not want to have conflicts with them. Because the situation was such that in the event of a major conflict, there could have been some far-reaching consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And those far-reaching consequences, are they the matters you're referring to at the end of this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Object on the leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I -- yes, Mr. President, I can rephrase the question if it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you just referred to there being far-reaching consequences. Could you just explain to the Court what the practical situation was and what the consequences may have been and how you sought to avoid conflicts that you referred to in your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: At this time, the situation was very tense and dangerous. Events that today would appear to be very simple, in those days, for those same events, people would draw their weapons. Therefore, we advised our men not to clash with armed -- with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, with uniformed men --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: -- to let the military police handle that, because more often than not, these were members of the HV who were demobilised and who were from this area who came to loot and take away items, and they would transport them away. And it was to be expected that they would shoot the civilian police because that's what the relationship was. I will just say something here by way of an example. They would frequently use the following sentence, Where were you while we were fighting? So in some ways they felt that they were above the Croatian police. Considering themselves -- considering the police, the civilian police, to be someone who came on the scene late when the job had already been done. So we told our policemen not to take any action because we could expect the worst to happen. We told them to let the military police to handle this. Fortunately, no such conflict occurred, materialized, but it was to be expected. It could be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. Now this situation that you've just described to the Court, did you report that situation to your superiors, Mr. Franjo and Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. They knew about these problems. My colleague Ivo Baric was supposed to and probably did talk to General Cermak about these problems at meetings that were being held on a nearly daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So in addition to General Cermak, did the reports also go to your superiors in Zagreb; namely, Mr. Moric or Mr. Franjo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Franjo certainly knew about these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit number D48 displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you'll see this is a document - if we can just show the author at the bottom there, Mr. Registrar - that is from Josko Moric, and it is addressed to the chief of the military police, Mr. Lausic. If you could just take a moment, and if could you read that document.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could refer you to the third paragraph, you'll see that there's a reference there to the problems that the civilian police face and the final sentence says: "The fact that the perpetrators wear HV uniforms completely blocks the work of the civilian police." Is that consistent with your experience in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I was talking about a minute ago. The problem was all the more difficult because soon after we had entered the liberated territory of Knin, a train passed through carrying President Tudjman and civilians were allowed into these recently liberated areas. Civilians were now arriving on a massive scale to go back to their homes, houses, and everyone wanted to take something from there. There was a lot of pressure at all these check-points, and we were being kept very busy. It was difficult with all of this going on to keep under control the problems that were being caused by persons wearing military uniforms, and this is precisely what Mr. Moric wanted to warn Mr. Lausic about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You have referred to the operation of the train, and also you've referred to the train carrying President Tudjman. And can you -- do you recall, is that what's been come to be known as the freedom train. Is that the reference that you're making there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And do you recall what date that was that the freedom train came to Knin, or when about in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. According to our assessments, the assessments that we, the police, made at the time, it was quite soon. It was between five and eight days after the territory had been penetrated. If you ask me, it was too soon because we were simply unable at this time to effectively cover the area, in security terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And do you recall that -- that any -- any issues arising once the train was operating, in relation to freedom of movement -- in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going object. I'm not sure what freedom of movement counsel refers to, if we could get more specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In your answer you referred to the fact that once the train passed through carrying civilians, there was -- civilians entered into the liberated territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I think probably the easiest way for me to proceed may be if I show the witness some documentation that may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a comment. I didn't rise before but I guess I will note it on the record now. A document of Mr. Moric was put to the witness and then he was asked, "Do you agree with this," which I think is a similar situation to where I think we had an agreement about putting statements of other witnesses to a witness before having asked the witness his opinion of certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in respect to this particular topic, I think counsel and I are aware there are two different dates that the witness is talking about and if before we show him a document we can ask him specifically which date he refers to, he talks about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've got to, obviously, be a little bit careful in terms of the submissions that we intend to make on this topic and maybe if the witness could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could -- if we go into the substance I think it would be wiser to ask the witness to take his earphones off. Mr. Buhin, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take your earphones off for a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think the essence of what is happening here is that the witness has mentioned the freedom train which travelled sometime in late August, around the 25th, 26th, if I'm not mistaken, but he's also simultaneously said that this issue arose five to eight days from when the police entered. So my objection is if we put a document to the witness regarding that date without first asking him to specify what does he mean, is he confused as to when the freedom train went through or is he consistent in his belief that the civilians came in three weeks after Operation Storm. That's the essence of what is at dispute here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then perhaps, Mr. Margetts, if you would follow the suggestion also heard as part of your question, the train carrying civilians, which I did not catch before. I don't know whether it was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think our position is also it was carrying dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Margetts, you mentioned -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was attempting to follow the witness's answer as closely as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not hear, as a matter of fact, but I could have missed that, that the train was carrying any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide me to the page and the line where --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just finding it now myself. I think the answer starts at page 32, line 5. The train passed through carrying President Tudjman and civilians were allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And civilians were allowed into this recently -- I never understood this to be a train passed through carrying President Tudjman and civilians, because then the next part of the sentence would be without a subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood a train passed through carrying President Tudjman and civilians were allowed into this recently liberated areas. I never understood the line to mean that the civilians were on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yes, thank you very much for that assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If could you please keep that in mind as well. Although a document is not exactly the same as taking the witness to a -- to the testimony of another witness, it -- nevertheless, it's always to be preferred to see whether the witness, even without the assistance of documents and testimony of other witnesses, could tell us anything about what he observed or knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: May I actually -- I did have a submission in relation to that and the use of D48. I would like to put it on the record that in terms of the use of that document, I think that the record will show there was a substantial development of this witness's knowledge, his reporting chain, his relationship with Mr. Moric, and the extent, therefore, to which those events were connected prior to the presentation of that document. So I'd say that that was an instance where I would hope that -- that the -- an adequate basis was presented for presentation of D48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll respond to that by saying I think that despite that foundation, there's still the need to put matters to a witness before you show him what somebody else wrote in a document that. So that would be our position on that. The other thing is a strictly technical matter, Your Honour. I think in the future, it would be wiser if instead of asking the witness to take off his earphones, we ask him to unplug the headphones from the set because I think there's still some audio coming through in terms of the translation. I hear the sound coming from the earphones. I just want to make sure that in the future we arrive at a common procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would not invite witnesses to plug out matters. We'd certainly need the assistance of the usher for that. Mr. Margetts, again, a lot of words. Do you think you could rephrase the question in such a way or put other questions first so that we could proceed after that without further interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put up your earphones again. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, we just had a technical discussion relating to some procedures in terms of the questions that I'll be presenting to you. Now a question relates to the issue of the travel of Mr. Tudjman to Knin on the freedom train, and I just wanted to ask you again just to be -- if you could again attend to the issue as to whether you could put some type of date on the date that Franjo Tudjman came in. Did he arrive in early August, middle August, later August, about -- about when? Are you able to assist the Court?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I'm unable to specify the date. It was at the beginning of August, three to five days after the entry -- three to eight, perhaps, at the very most, after we entered Knin, and I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, are you able to assist the Court as to when the train was again operating and was entering Knin after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I can't give you the date. But from our security perspective, it certainly was too early. But I can't say when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your security perspective, what types of freedom of movement did persons have in the area of Knin? Were you aware that -- did people need to hold passes, did people need to register themselves with authorities? What was the situation in terms of freedom of movement for people in the area of the Kotar-Knin jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I can't remember any details, but based on my recollection, I think that in the first days everyone needed proof of the fact that they were natives of the area and I think they were given some passes. I'm not sure who issued those, the army, or the civilian authorities. Soon after, perhaps three to five days later, it was open to all those who wished to enter the area, and no passes were required. That's as specific as I can get on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, at the check-points that you were administering, were your policemen checking to see whether or not people had passes to enter the area and allowing those that had the passes and not allowing those that didn't?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Probably the answer is yes, but I don't remember any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, it's obviously been some time since you were dealing with these issues. Would it assist you if I was able to present some documents to you, relating to that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I don't believe so. We can give it a try, if you like, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Give it a try anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If, Mr. Registrar, I could please present Exhibit D494 to Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buhin, you'll see that this is a document from Ivo Cipci. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I see now that he was chief of the -- or, rather, head of the administration, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please refer to the second page of the B/C/S. And you'll see there -- have you seen this pass before, Mr. Buhin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I probably have, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could please move to another document that may be of some assistance. That's Exhibit D496.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I've got another document here, Mr. Buhin, from Mr. Cipci. And you will see it's a document dated 15th of August, 1995. And in fact it refers in the first paragraph there, you'll see -- in fact, just if you could read the document and I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is this the circumstance that you were referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think a foundation needs to be laid, Your Honour, before the witness gives his opinion on a document such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have also circulated an e-mail specifically to address the freedom train issue before the next break, so before we head down a path which I think is going to lead to much more confusion. Either that, or to ask the witness again to unplug his headset and I will explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you unplug the headset of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think our position is that the confusion here arises because the witness is aware that the president was in Knin within three to five days of Operation Storm, he is just mistaken about how he got to Knin, whether it was by the train, which was the second trip at the end of the August, or by helicopter on the 6th. So before we veer off on the path of trying to convince the witness that civilians couldn't come in until the freedom train which was three weeks later, I think our position would be that he was simply mistaken about the means that the president arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties agree on the first arrival not being by train. The second arrival being by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We certainly agree to those two facts in terms of attempting to assist the Court. In terms of this witness's evidence, I think we may have a different view. It seemed to us -- well, it seemed to me that the answer related to the return of civilians, and I think it is helpful in light of that, in light of this witness's central position in terms of overseeing the operations in Kotar-Knin that we be as precise as we can, in terms of understanding what he is referring to, when he is referring to that return of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand, Mr. Misetic, that you would not object against Mr. Margetts leading on arrivals by train or by any other means of transportation so in order to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As my friend -- I think we can probably stipulate on when the train came, I think it is the 26th. What I don't want to have happen is that the witness has already, I think twice now, said that the problem with civilians arriving was three to eight days, I think he said three to five, something like that, from their arrival on the scene, so that we don't try to convince the witness that because he referred to the train he must be mistaken as to when the civilians started to arrive. Rather, I would just put it to him rather than moving to impeach him on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is this a suggestion that could you live with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The -- I think it is important in terms of addressing this issue with the witness a number of years subsequent to the events, 13 years later, that he have as many contemporaneous materials as we possibly can present to him to assist him in terms of placing himself back at that time, and if ever I would submit there was an opportunity for that, it's the opportunity that arises with this particular series of documents that assist him in terms of the issuing of passes, in terms of the impact of those passes, and in terms of the relevance of those passes to the increased number of civilians. I fear that if we proceed and we attempt to elicit the evidence freely from the witness without assisting him here that possibly that evidence will not be of great value to the Chamber. So I -- I don't see -- I see that he is the perfect person being centrally placed in regard to these particular events to comment on these materials, and that's the reason I proceeded in this way because I understood that that would provide quality evidence to the Chamber. And it was for the very reason that I thought the evidence we were receiving was less than the greatest quality given the number of years that I've sought to proceed with the documentation rather than merely asking open questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is that of course it is what you put to the witness, and so I wonder if my colleague would have shown him a video of Tudjman in Knin on the 6th, and then to say did you mean that he helicoptered in on the 6th, or go down a path where the Prosecution is only going to show him documents to suggest to him that he is wrong about the date of the train and when civilians came. I believe that the documents are what they are. And that actually the value of calling witnesses in testimony is to first check on what they know on the basis of questions posed. And rather than doing what the Prosecution is proposing to do, which by another name, is called leading him, using documents to lead him to a certain conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand. What you want to establish, Mr. Margetts, is when the civilians started to return is that -- or when they were returning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. When they were returning in sufficient numbers to -- to be relevant through the answer that he provided and the context that he gave to that return of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see whether we can find out whether the witness has any recollection. Because he arrived Knin immediately after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, he arrived immediately after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether he can come any further. Could the earphones be plugged in again. Mr. Buhin. Mr. Buhin, you told us about civilians returning to the area; do you remember that? Now, could you describe when did the civilians start returning to the area, and could you please tell us that in relation to the moment you arrived in Knin? Was it after three days, seven days, ten days? When did the civilians return, or start returning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, civilians started returning after the arrival of the freedom train. That's what it was called. Those were the first arrivals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said they started returning after the arrival of the freedom train, and I think that -- now, do you remember approximately how many days after you arrived that the freedom train arrived in Knin? Was that after three days, seven days, ten days, two weeks, four weeks? Could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps seven to ten days later. I can't be certain, but it must be in that ballpark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say that it was a certain number of days after you arrived, are you actually referring to the arrival of Mr. Tudjman when you're talking about the freedom train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as I remember, he was among the people on that train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first train to arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that Mr. Tudjman came to Knin during that month of August twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first time he was helicoptered into the area. I think that was on day two, following our arrival. He went up as far as the flag that was flown above Knin. He was there for the hoisting of the flag, and he left soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the return of the civilians, you said, was -- started only after the freedom train arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not any earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Due to the short break that we took ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- I have some thoughts. We had a relatively long break but almost immediately after the -- after the start of this hearing. I would suggest, with the -- unless I hear strong protests from the booth -- that we have a break at 20 minutes to 5.00, have then a little bit a longer break, until 20 minutes past 5.00 and then continue until 7.00, so that we have relatively long sessions but also relatively long breaks. It also allows the witness to read again his statement during the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if we forget about it, the tape will stop us anyhow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, we were discussing until we talked about the various -- about the various times of arrival of Mr. Tudjman. We were discussing effectively the role of the military police and the role of the civilian police. And you indicated in your statement the fact that there were separate check-points, and you also various other aspects of the civilian police's interaction with the military police. Just to assist you further and to develop this topic a little further, I would like to present to you some instructions that were issued in February of 1993 by Mate Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have D510 presented on the screen, and it's page 4 of the Croatian and the -- and it's also page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I'd like you to refer to -- yeah, if we could move -- if we could move on, Mr. Registrar, to page 4 of the B/C/S, which is the section 5. So, yes, that bottom part there. Mr. Buhin, you will see on the left-hand side of the screen section 5, and that relates to means of coercion which is the topic we've been talking about in terms of the civilian police's role with military personnel. And if you could read that section, section 5, and when you're ready if could you indicate to Mr. Registrar who can turn the page over.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I'm ready to turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the remainder, that's correct, just the remainder of section 5, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. This section refers to when the civilian police are authorised to take action against military police -- sorry, against military personnel. And that is only if no possibility of securing timely intervention by military authorities exists. Now, in the first full sentence that you see on the top of page 5, so four lines down, it says that for legal implementation of the means of coercion against a military person it is essential to find out whether it was possible for the military police to have intervened in a timely manner. My question to you is: In the circumstances that you've described today, where you had separate check-points and you were attempting to work with the military police with various success, were there circumstances where it was possible for the military police to intervene but they failed to do so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I can't remember any such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have some doubt about this document. We all can see that this document is dated by February 1993. Could we first establish whether this document was still applicable in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course you can seek to clarify that. Let me -- we're talking more or less about the interpretation of the document rather than about the document itself. The document being a Defence exhibit; is that -- or let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a Defence document, so therefore I think that perhaps some consultation with your colleagues or -- and if there is any issue that arises from it, of course you are free to raise it. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we could take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we'll resume a little bit later than usual, that is 20 minutes past 5. Mr. Buhin, could you please go through the document again and try to identify where you have developed a different opinion or assessment on what you said at that time, so that we can hear from you after the break. We resume at 20 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, could you assist us in telling us what the result is of having read, again, your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read the statement briefly, and there are two things that I would like to touch upon. On page 5, toward the top of the page, the fourth paragraph, it states while I was employed in the liberated territory, I saw vehicles, HVO vehicles, which in my opinion, transported looted items. When stopped they would show documents, proving that this was for the needs of the HV army. I believe that many of these documents were forged. I think that I would not say that anymore, because the items that were transported in the Croatian army vehicles, I believe, they were for the needs of the Croatian army. It is possible that in a small number of cases, this was abused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say, I no longer belief that many of these documents were forged but that sometimes such documents may have been abused. Yes. Was that the first issue you wanted to draw our attention to, or is there more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 6, the second paragraph ends with the following sentence, And the cooperation with the army was very poor. I don't know whether that is what I said at the time, probably not, because we had good cooperation with the military. We had daily meetings with them, and we had good cooperation with them. There were problems at first with the military police, but that is something that we've already discussed at length today. Later on, toward the end of my term, the check-points were joint check-points, or combined military police and civilian police check-points, and the cooperation had much improved. This statement as stated here doesn't sound very nice that was probably not what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your correction is on the record. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same page, the second paragraph from the bottom, the government through the ministry assigned us the task of protecting property and civilians, but it was impossible to do our job while the army was still there. I don't know how this sentence can stand as formulated. Maybe it was taken out of context because I'm sure that the army could not have different orders. Rather, I think it was, as we discussed it early today, that at the beginning, at least, in those in those first couple of days, uniformed men wilfully looted and torched other people's property. It is a fact - that's what it says in the last sentence - that military persons left that area earlier -- or had they left that area earlier, it would have been much easier for us, because these uniformed men would not then hide behind them and commit crimes. And I would like to stress one more time that I'm certain that there was no order. To the contrary, and that these were civilians who actually were -- who actually were prone to crime. Everything else could remain as standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just in relation to your last -- is that your opinion that it must have been civilians, or did you verify that all those, as you said, were involved in looting and torching were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I learned subsequently, in conversations with my colleagues from the crime police, in cases where the perpetrators were discovered, in most of those cases, these were individuals who were dressed in uniforms but were not members of any unit, or they were members of the Croatian army demobilised at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you learned later from your colleagues. Is that understood well? So it is not your permanent investigation that revealed that, but you learned that from those who did investigate? Now apart from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from these corrections that you made and the corrections you made earlier today, apart from them, does the statement accurately reflect what you said at the time; that is, in September 2001 and March 2002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, again, apart from the corrections you just made, did you give your statement in accordance with what was the truth, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you give the same answers if the same questions would be put to you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the attestation under Rule 92 ter is complete. Has a number already been assigned to the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not. May I take it that you tender it, and may I invite Mr. Registrar to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Therefore, P963 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, in the course of the corrections that you have just made to your statement and in the statement itself, you refer to the fact that the military police refuse to set up joint check-points. I'd like to present a document to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, if I could please have D49 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Buhin, this is another order from Mr. Moric we saw earlier a correspondence from Mr. Moric of the 17th of August, and this is it an order from Mr. Moric from the 18th of August. My first question is: Are you familiar with this document? Do you recall -- and take your time to have a look at it, but that will be my first question, whether or not you're familiar with this document. And obviously once you have finished reading the first page, if could you indicate and we'll turn the page over.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Could I please see the second page. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you recall this order being issued in -- on the 18th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I recall that there was an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
