utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 3 there, item 3, it's an item that refers to the establishment or request for mixed check-points. Does that item there reflect the issue that you raised in your statement, the refusal of the military police to engage in those mixed check-points?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going object to the question because I don't think that is the testimony of the witness. It assumes facts not in evidence, and I think the witness clarified that point earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm looking at page 5 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue, could you perhaps -- whether it was a refusal that's -- it -- at least it is -- it's leading, Mr. Margetts, if you could phrase the question in such a way that the leading element is taken out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you'll see that the issue of joint check-points is addressed in item 3 of the order. And --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You stated in your statement that you asked to have joint check-points - and this is on page 5 of your statement - with the military police but they refused. Now, as at the 18th of August, was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I believe that this order is the result of what I mentioned. We pointed out that there is a need for this, and following this, we had joint check-points. The military police made an agreement with the civilian police and the check-points were combined or unified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, as at the 18th of August, how would you assess the extent of the crime that was taking place on the territory? When I refer to crime, I refer to major incidents, such as burning of houses, major looting, and those type of incidents. As at the 18th of August, how would you assess the level of that crime?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I don't know if I can do that. I can't even give you an approximation after all these years, an approximate assessment. I think that at this time, we had far fewer problems with persons in uniforms that we were already beginning to have problems with citizens who were coming to this area to loot, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: -- take away whether it was their own property or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We've dealt with them in terms of identification and those issues. I'm just asking you that regardless of who perpetrated the crime, just the extent of the crime that you were observing in your role as a coordinator, you were present in the region, if you would -- could you describe to the Trial Chamber, the extent of the crime that was taking place, the looting and the burning and other incidents.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I don't know that I can explain and describe what the extent of those incidents were. There were incidents of looting and torching, but for every house that was torched, for us, it was one house too many. I don't know if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to ask you and I don't -- and you have certainly answered me, but I would like to give you one other opportunity maybe to attempt to quantify that for the Trial Chamber. Was it one house, was it a hundred houses, was it a thousand houses, was it extensive, was it obvious? What was the extent of the crime that you were observing that was taking place, in terms of the looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Well, my answer to that question would be there were some incidents or if I were to try to be more precise, in every hamlet maybe there were one, two, or at most three houses that were torched. There wasn't widespread torching, but even this was too many cases for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could just refer you again to you D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, if you refer back to the first page in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Because Mr. Moric states in the third paragraph that: "The torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's property has assumed such proportions that it is inflicting political damage on the Republic of Croatia ..." What's your reaction to that assessment of the extent of the crime?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: If we go back to what I said before, that every hamlet had one or two houses torched in this wide-liberated area, that was -- that would have been a rather large number, and it is certain that this was causing damage to the reputation of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in terms of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry there's a part of his answer at the end I don't think that the interpreter was able to hear, so if we could ask him to repeat the last portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Buhin, what we have on the record is now is that after you explained that one or two houses were torched in every hamlet in a wide area, that would be a rather large number and that it is certain that this was causing damage to the reputation of the Republic of Croatia. Then apparently you added something. Could you tell what you said after you said: "... damage to the reputation of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the reputation of the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So we've looked at these reports of -- correspondence from Moric, the 17 August letter and this 18 August letter, and you've indicated that they reflect some of the concerns that -- that you had as well. Now, in terms of your capacity to address the crime that was taking place, how did the refusal of the military police to engage in joint check-points impact on your capacity to address this crime?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I think that this did not create major problems. The only thing is we could not observe and monitor everything that was being taken out or transported out of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So in terms of items that were transported out by the military, your -- what was your capacity to observe that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: There weren't any, or there wasn't any capacity. Whatever was taken out was in enclosed vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in terms of the -- you've described the fact that check-points were set up separately. To what extent were you able to observe the conduct of those check-points by the military police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: We could not observe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. I'd like to move on to another topic. And that's relating to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I have some difficulties in understanding. You told us earlier, isn't it, that the military police would have a check-point at a distance of 10 or 20 metres of the civilian police. And you have described how documents were shown, and now you say you were not certain. There may have been some abuse of those documents, but you wouldn't say that that was often the case. Now, isn't that a description of how the military police handled these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information was probably reached or we probably gained insight into this after the contacts between my colleague Ivo Baric and his meeting with General Cermak and representatives of the military police, these meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so this is where we learned about this. But the civilian police did not check military vehicles. And all that I can add now in view of how much time that has passed I cannot really confirm any details, but I believe that in those cases where military persons were found in vehicles without any plates or in civilian vehicles that they were being intercepted and they had to show their documents to show that they were driving or transporting these items for the needs of the army, and I believe that some, a small number probably, of these documents were false, but at that time it was difficult to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you could observe what happened at the check-points of the military police because you're now describing it. Mr. Margetts earlier asked you to what extent you were able to observe the conduct of the check-points of the military police, and your answer was, We could not observe this, whereas you now give quite a description of what happened at these check-points, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we could not actually follow as to what the military police did. We could not monitor that. In case where these were military personnel, they were within the competence of the military police and then we had no follow-up as to what happened subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, for example, you could see whether the check-point would take over the goods that were transported, or whether those who were transporting those goods were let through and could continue their way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. But we didn't have anything written down or anything registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question by Mr. Margetts was not what you registered but whether you could observe what happened at the check-points manned by the military police. You changed your mind, to some extent, from that you said that these were mainly forged documents, but now you say, Well, I'm not -- I can't say that anymore at this moment. I've reconsidered that. Now, what in first instance did make you believe that these might be forged documents; and what makes you believe that in some instances abuse of the documents could have been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably from the practice itself, and based on what was being done then and what was being transported then, it is certain that there were instances where some individuals using military uniforms looted and drove away those goods for their own needs. That was difficult to determine because it was not within our competence to investigate what was forged documents and what was not. But I am sure that some of them were forged. I don't have any evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you also said based on what was being done and what was being transported then. Now, could you tell us what was transported then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever could be loaded onto a truck or a car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, household appliances, window-frames, doors, anything that was movable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few ... I think I'm just trying to find it. One of your previous answers said that this was all loaded on covered and not open trucks. How could you observe what was transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally I didn't see almost anything because I spent most of my time in my office. But in conversations with police officers, when I went to inspect the check-points, I was told by the police officers about what was being transported. What -- as far as they could see, most of these items were transported in covered vehicles, but there were also some open vehicles, a small number, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I'd just like to move on to another topic and that is you refer in your statement and you have mentioned it in -- in passing some of your answers today the fact that Mr. Romanic and Mr. Baric had daily meetings with General Cermak. And you indicated in your statement that after these meetings Romanic and Baric would discuss the results of meetings with you, and you also said that they would return, we would discuss what had gone on at the meeting, and plan our day accordingly. In terms of the conclusions that were reached at those meetings that were communicated to you, did you implement those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: We did, certainly, to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the -- the conclusions that were implemented, did they include issues of freedom of movement in the area of the Kotar-Knin -- freedom of movement of civilians in the Kotar-Knin ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And do you recall implementing any decisions relating to that, that emanated from these daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I can't mention a single one off the bat. I don't know what specifically you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. I just thought I may refer you to an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'd like to refer to a document that is under seal. So if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you'll see here that there's an order here from General Cermak and it's date the 15th of August, 1995. And it refers to the freedom of movement of civilians. And you will see down there that it is addressed to the Knin police station and the Knin military police. This document here, is this the type of document you would see the -- Romanic and Baric return from the daily meetings with and have you seen documents of this nature before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we see if he has seen this document, Your Honour. We're dealing with a specific document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question by one. So first, have you -- Mr. Buhin, have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you don't remember in terms of this specific document, dealing with the movement of civilians? You don't remember seeing this document. In terms of these documents generally, did Mr. Romanic and Mr. Baric return with documents after their meetings with Mr. -- with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I don't remember noticing anything like that. Normally we would just talk about what had been discussed at any meetings that preceded the situations. It has been a long time and I find myself unable to recollect details of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. But seeing this document, is this consistent with the types of issues and information that they would convey to you when they met with you after these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Looking at this document, I don't know who the General ordered to act in keeping with this document, or was this simply forwarded to the civilian police and the military police in Knin just by way of information. I believe that we used our own chain of command to coordinate with the Minister of the Interior following something like this and then Mr. Cedo Romanic's order would have followed. I don't consider this to be a direct order to the police. After all, if you look at the addressees, there's nothing there, really. We don't know who the order is to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, again, the witness hasn't answered your question, and I prefer that he does so. The question was put to you, Mr. Buhin, whether the subject matter of what appears in this document, whether that is the kind of issues that they would convey to you as matters being discussed at the meetings you have told us about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This must have been a topic that was raised at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what you learned from those that participated in those meetings, that these were the kind of topics that were discussed during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably so. I don't know of any other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic, Mr. Buhin, and that is the issue of crime investigation. And we've dealt with that earlier today to some extent when we talked about the Official Note that you -- that recorded or purported to record a meeting you had with the Republic of Croatia, Ministry of the Interior. And you have addressed it also in your witness statement. And that is that the process was, and I'm confirming what is in your witness statement, that as I understand it, when an incident of crime came to your attention, you reported that to the Zadar police administration, and we dealt with the specific incident of -- the Grubori incident, and you indicated that you reported that to Ivica Cetina, to the best of your recollection. Did you also report these matters directly to the chief of the criminal police, in Zadar, Mr. Ive Kardum?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And so how would you -- you say not directly. Did you understand he received these reports from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. I'm going to object at this point because there is no foundation here and I'm having a hard time following. If we could first establish what report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What are the reports, when did he prepare them, what are we talking about, and was this when did you forward them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that the question is assuming a kind of report which has not been identified yet. At the same time, if someone says there was no -- it was not reported directly, that suggests that this is an indirect reporting and I took it that what Mr. Margetts was referring to. Perhaps we just ask the witness -- You said it was not directly -- the question was: "Did you already report these matters directly to the chief of the criminal police in Zadar, Mr. Ive Kardum." You said, "Not directly." Now tell us, if it was not directly, what then happened that makes you say that it was not reported directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed it was sufficient to inform the chief of the police administration, Mr. Ivo Cetina, and I'm sure he knew about what was going on. He promised that he would set up a team for an on-site inspection and make sure there was an investigating judge there. He also promised to dispatch them to Knin. At this point, there was no further need for me to check whether he had, in fact, done that or had informed the chief of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- I put on the record that I assume from the answer that we're talking specifically about the Grubori incident and not how the system functioned generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was another problem in the question that you started with the Grubori incident and then you enlarged the subject of your question. Mr. -- precision here also avoids a lot of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the balance I'm trying to strike here is, instead of going straight to specific paragraphs of the witness's statement, I'm trying to strike a balance between taking information that we're all familiar with in his statement and developing it without needing to take the compass and technique of specific reference, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that you explain what you were doing, Mr. Margetts. We observe what you were doing, and we also observe what then happens. This is not to encourage the Defence to object against every question, but it certainly also encourages you, Mr. Margetts, to phrase your questions in such a way, and I would add to that, to introduce them in such a way that Mr. Misetic or the others have not even a chance to object. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could please have the witness's statement presented. It's now P963. And if we could refer to page 3 of the B/C/S and to -- it's page 4 of the English, the first paragraph. Page 3 of the B/C/S, if we go down to the bottom of that page, Mr. Registrar. It's the last paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, you'll see in that -- the start, the first part of that last paragraph, you refer generally to the procedure that you engaged in. And that -- the general procedure of reporting to the Zadar criminal police. You state that it was usually Romanic or Mihic who reported it and sometimes you or Baric would go directly to Ivica Cetina. Just referring to the system that was in place in August 1995, I am interested to know, in August 1995, were there criminal policemen who were in Knin, were they working, for example, at the elementary school or otherwise; and if you do know of any criminal policemen that were in Knin in August 1995, would you be able to give the Trial Chamber their names?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: No. The crime police were not in Knin. There were none in Knin, in fact. They were in Zadar. As far as work in the Knin area was concerned, we would always have crime policemen from Zadar come over and then they would take care of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And these crime policemen from Zadar, were some of them taking care of tasks that were performed in the elementary school where people had gathered?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know -- is the name Slavko Raspovic familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I'd now like to move on to another topic, a related topic but another topic, nonetheless, and that is the matter of the Grubori investigation that we've already touched on today. Now, you indicated earlier when we were addressing the Official Note you had informed probably Ivica Cetina of the -- of the incident that had taken place, and I'd just like to refer you to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Registrar, we've got it up on the screen. And if we could go to page 4 of the B/C/S, and that's page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And about two-thirds of the way down, you refer to the issues of the conversation with Sacic and the steps that had been taken. And you said that it had been agreed to have an investigating judge come from Zadar with the criminal police to investigate and try the killings. Are you able to identify any of the people from the prosecutor`s office or otherwise who had been -- who were going to come down and investigate the killings? Do you recall who they were or what their names were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I never knew their names. I don't know who they were. I don't know who the prosecutors were in Zadar at the time. The job itself was left to the chief of the police administration, Ivo Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So up to that point, had you been present when any investigations had been conducted by the criminal police or the prosecutors in the area, or hadn't you been present and, therefore, hadn't you had the opportunity to meet these people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: Do you mean the Grubori incident or some other situations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm just referring generally to your knowledge of the personnel who were operating either engaged by the prosecutors's office or engaged by the Zadar criminal police. At that stage, had you had the opportunity to meet any of those persons.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN
utterances.text: I am certain that I did not meet any prosecutors or investigating judges. As to members of the crime police, if indeed I met some of them, the one thing I can tell you is I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I need to deal with two exhibits that are under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session and the exhibits not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
